title: The principle of relativity and the Lorentz transformation
summary: The principle of relativity; relativity of simultaneity (the train) and invariance of transverse dimensions; proof of the invariance of the interval with the light clock; linearity and the derivation of the Lorentz transformation; time dilation, simultaneity shifts and length contraction as corollaries; rapidity, hyperbolic rotation and velocity addition.

objectives.description: Prove the invariance of the interval from the principle of relativity and the invariance of transverse dimensions, naming where each hypothesis is used.
Derive the Lorentz transformation from linearity and the invariance of the interval, check its units and its Galilean limit, and invert it.
Obtain time dilation, the quantitative relativity of simultaneity and length contraction from the transformation, stating the simultaneity condition that defines a length measurement.
Write a boost as a hyperbolic rotation by the rapidity, prove that rapidities add, and derive the velocity-addition law.

preparation.description: Read Section 3.1 The Principle of Relativity (pp. 53–55) and skim Sections 3.2–3.3 (pp. 56–61) on what is and is not the same in different frames.
Read Section 3.4 Relativity of Simultaneity (pp. 62–63), Einstein's train, and Section 3.5 Lorentz Contraction of Length (pp. 63–64), noting the insistence on measurement rather than sight.
Read Section 3.6 Invariance of Transverse Dimension (pp. 65–67): the wheels and the pipes.
Read Section 3.7 Invariance of the Interval Proved (pp. 67–70) with Table 3-1, and Section 3.8 (pp. 71–72) for the super-rocket check. Redo the 3-4-5 arithmetic in our sign convention.

Read Special Topic L.3–L.5 (pp. 99–101): the clock at the rocket origin and γ, why the transformation is linear, and the completion of the derivation; then the result (L-10) and the inverse transformation (p. 102).
Read Special Topic L.7 Addition of Velocities (pp. 103–110).
Second account: Tong, Dynamics and Relativity, Section 7.1 Lorentz Transformations and Section 7.3.2 The Lorentz Group (reference-only; signature (+,−,−,−)).

activities.title: Lecture: from the principle to the transformation
activities.instructions: Read the lesson with Chapter 3 and the Special Topic. Reproduce the derivation of the Lorentz transformation on paper without the book, then compare coefficient by coefficient with Eqs. (L-6)–(L-10). Optional: MIT 8.20 Week 2 videos (Lecture 4.4 Invariance, 4.5 Lorentz Transformation, 5.2 Velocity Addition).

activities.title: Tutorial: the boost as a hyperbolic rotation; a paradox in two frames
activities.instructions: Attempt exercise 1 before asking for any hint. Then attempt exercise 2, drawing the two events in both frames before computing. Submit each attempt when you believe it is complete; revise after feedback.

activities.title: Explain: a boost is a rotation by a hyperbolic angle
activities.instructions: Write exercise 3 without the sources open, then compare with Tong's rotational analogy (Section 7.3.1).

activities.title: Retrieval: the transformation and its corollaries
activities.instructions: From memory: the Lorentz transformation and its inverse with c explicit; γ; the three corollaries with their conditions (clock at rest in S′; Δt = 0 in S; ends measured at the same S-time); the rapidity and the velocity-addition law.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: the Lorentz transformation derived from linearity and invariance, written as a hyperbolic rotation, composition shown to add rapidities, velocity addition derived, units and the Galilean limit checked.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Lorentz contraction is what a moving object looks like.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It is the result of measuring both ends at the same time in the observer's frame with a lattice of clocks; what an eye sees also includes light-travel delays and is a different question (book, pp. 63–64).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Time dilation and length contraction are additional postulates.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Both follow from the Lorentz transformation, which follows from linearity and the invariance of the interval, which follows from the principle of relativity and transverse invariance (Sections 3.7, L.3–L.5).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Velocities add: a projectile fired forward at u from a ship moving at v travels at u + v.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Rapidities add; velocities combine as w = (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²), which is less than c whenever u and v are (Section L.7).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Each observer thinks the other's clocks run slow, which is a contradiction.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Each compares a proper time (one clock) with a coordinate time (two synchronised clocks), and the two comparisons concern different pairs of events; the symmetry is required by the principle of relativity and involves no contradiction (unit 4 draws the diagram).
